articles.headline: China's Factories Report 14.4% Profit Jump, Mostly From Selling Shovels to the AI Gold Rush
articles.dek: Industrial profits grew at their fastest pace since June, but the same data shows Chinese households are mostly not invited to the party.
articles.catch_up: China's National Bureau of Statistics released September industrial profit figures on Tuesday. They show earnings recovering after three straight years of declines, driven by AI-related equipment, even as consumer demand remains weak.
articles.why_it_matters: The data shows that China's growth is leaning heavily on global AI spending and exports rather than its own shoppers, which leaves it exposed if that spending slows. For everyone else, it suggests the AI buildout is feeding real factory profits well beyond the chip companies themselves.
body: Profits at large Chinese industrial firms rose 14.4% in September from a year earlier, the strongest pace since June, according to data released Tuesday by the National Bureau of Statistics, as reported by CNBC. For the first nine months of the year, profits are up 15.5%. This is a considerable recovery for a sector that, until last year, had spent three consecutive years shrinking.

The explanation is that the world is building AI data centers, and someone has to make the parts. Chief Statistician Yu Weining pointed to electronics and advanced manufacturing, where makers of electronic special materials saw profits more than triple, and semiconductor equipment makers saw a 51.7% jump. Translation: when everyone is panning for gold, the shovel factory has a very good quarter.

The shovels go further down the aisle than one might expect. Profits at optical fiber manufacturers rose more than sixfold over the nine months, and cable makers more than doubled, according to Yu. Copper and aluminum producers gained nearly 45%, helped by demand from AI and renewable industries. CNBC also notes that higher commodity prices stemming from the war in Iran have lifted earnings at miners and raw-material suppliers.

That last point comes with a catch. Downstream manufacturers, the ones who buy those materials and turn them into things, are facing rising input costs. Their customers, meanwhile, are not exactly queuing up. Earnings growth in AI and robotics is outpacing clothing, autos and furniture, which is the economic equivalent of the cafeteria having excellent steak and no one at the salad bar being paid.

The weak link is the Chinese household. Retail sales grew just 1.1% in September, which beat forecasts but was only marginally above August's weak reading. Shena Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said the property downturn continues to weigh on housing purchases and related durables, and that "China's export strength isn't able to fully offset its domestic weakness." Translation: selling to the world is working, and selling to the neighbors is not.

The broader numbers are respectable on paper. The economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, slightly faster than the previous quarter, bringing nine-month growth to 4.6%, within the government's full-year target of 4.5% to 5%. Profit growth also owes something to Beijing's efforts to curb price wars, which is the policy of asking companies to stop selling things at a loss in the hope that they will stop.

As for help, CNBC reports that Beijing has so far held back from major new stimulus for domestic demand, citing concerns over local government debt and the fading effect of consumer trade-in subsidies. So the plan, for now, is to let the AI boom carry the load. What to watch is whether global data center spending keeps its pace, since the factories are currently depending on customers abroad who, like all enthusiasts, may eventually run out of room for more cable.
articles.wire_headline: China industrial profits post strongest growth in three months, rising 14.4%

articles.headline: DoorDash Eyes Instacart in $17 Billion Bid to Out-Deliver Walmart and Amazon
articles.dek: The Wall Street Journal reports the two delivery middlemen are in advanced talks, in a deal that would value Instacart at roughly $17 billion.
articles.catch_up: DoorDash, which brings restaurant food to your door, is reportedly in advanced talks to buy Instacart, which brings groceries to your door. MarketWatch reports analysts see the move as a response to pressure from Walmart and Amazon.
articles.why_it_matters: If the deal happens, two of the biggest names in app-based delivery would become one, which could affect the fees, prices and choices shoppers see when ordering groceries online. It also shows that even large platforms feel pressure from retailers that own the shelves, the trucks and the customer.
body: DoorDash was in advanced talks to buy Instacart in a deal that would value the grocery delivery company at roughly $17 billion, according to the Wall Street Journal, as relayed by MarketWatch. No deal has been announced in the material provided, and talks described as advanced have been known to end the way most dates described as going well do.

MarketWatch reports that analysts see the logic as defensive: keeping up with Walmart and Amazon. Translation: the two largest retailers already own the warehouses, the delivery fleets and the customer relationships, while DoorDash and Instacart rent access to other people's stores. Merging two rented businesses does not create an owned one, but it does create a larger one, which in corporate strategy is often treated as the same thing.

The appeal of a combination is fairly mechanical. DoorDash has customers who order dinner, and Instacart has customers who order the groceries they were presumably going to cook before they ordered dinner. Combine them and, in theory, one app handles both the failed intention and the backup plan. The sources provided do not give deal terms beyond the reported valuation, so questions of price per share, cash versus stock, and regulatory review remain open.

That last item matters. Antitrust regulators tend to take notice when one of the largest players in a niche buys another, and a deal between two leading delivery apps would presumably invite questions about competition. The sources do not say how regulators might respond, so any forecast would be speculation, a commodity the markets already produce in abundance.

The backdrop is not especially relaxed. The latest data show CPI inflation at 3.74% year over year as of September, and the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.0% as of October 23. Translation: groceries cost more, and borrowing to buy things costs more too. The Fed funds rate sits at 3.88%, so a $17 billion purchase is being contemplated in a world where money is not free, though it is considerably cheaper for those who can afford a $17 billion purchase.

Markets, meanwhile, are in a reasonably calm mood. The SPY exchange-traded fund, which tracks the S&P 500, stood at 765.37 on October 26, and the VIX, a gauge of expected market swings, was 19.45 on October 23. That is not panic, which leaves room for deals that might otherwise be considered too ambitious.

What to watch is whether the talks become an announcement, and whether regulators or customers object. Shoppers will likely learn the outcome the usual way: through a new fee that arrives with an explanation about enhanced value.
articles.wire_headline: A possible DoorDash-Instacart deal is all about keeping up with Walmart and Amazon, analysts say
